relationship: named royal commission and narrative counterpart
rationale: Isaiah names Cyrus as the ruler whose hand God grasps to subdue nations. Ezra names Cyrus, attributes his kingdoms and Jerusalem commission to the Lord, and records the proclamation enabling the return. Ezra does not repeat the anointing language.

relationship: close verbal parallel in shattered barriers
rationale: Both attribute the shattering of bronze gates or doors and the breaking of iron bars to God. Isaiah applies the imagery to the way opened before Cyrus; the psalm praises divine deliverance.

relationship: internal divine calling by name
rationale: The God who calls Cyrus by name in Isaiah 45 also tells Jacob and Israel that He called them by name in Isaiah 43. The recipients differ; the repeated personal summons belongs to the same God's purposeful action.

relationship: internal identification of the chosen servant
rationale: Isaiah 45 explains Cyrus's call by reference to God's servant Jacob and chosen Israel. Isaiah 41 explicitly calls Israel and Jacob God's chosen servant and describes taking and calling that servant.

relationship: shared declaration of divine uniqueness
rationale: Isaiah declares that the Lord is God with none besides Him, despite Cyrus's lack of knowledge. Deuteronomy uses the same exclusive declaration as the knowledge Israel should gain from God's acts.

relationship: shared worldwide recognition from sunrise to sunset
rationale: Both use the span from the sun's rising to its setting for recognition of the Lord among peoples. Isaiah emphasizes knowing there is no other God; Malachi emphasizes His glorified name and worship.

relationship: divine agency in calamity
rationale: Isaiah expressly says that God makes peace and creates calamities. Amos similarly asks whether a calamity occurs in a city without the Lord doing it. Neither connection requires replacing calamities with a claim that God commits moral wrongdoing.

relationship: creation of light and ordering of darkness
rationale: Isaiah identifies God as the One fashioning light and making darkness. Genesis narrates God's command bringing light and His division and naming of light and darkness within creation.

relationship: shared heavenly and earthly growth imagery
rationale: Isaiah calls clouds to sprinkle righteousness and earth to produce mercy and righteousness. The psalm likewise joins mercy and righteousness with truth springing from earth, righteousness looking from heaven, and the land yielding fruit.

relationship: potter and clay objection parallel
rationale: Both challenge the formed thing's questioning of its maker through potter-and-clay imagery. Romans develops the potter's authority over vessels; Isaiah also includes the plower question and must not be reduced to Romans's wording.

relationship: creation of earth and the heavenly array
rationale: Isaiah attributes earth, its humanity, heaven and the commanded stars to God's hand. Nehemiah's prayer likewise names the Lord alone as maker of heaven and its array, earth and everything in it.

relationship: royal return and Jerusalem rebuilding counterpart
rationale: Isaiah describes a divinely raised king rebuilding God's city and releasing His people's captivity. Ezra records Cyrus directing God's people to return to Jerusalem and build the temple. It supplies the return-and-building counterpart without independently repeating the no-ransom clause.

relationship: bowing with recognition of God's presence
rationale: Isaiah's arriving peoples bow and acknowledge that God is in the one addressed. Paul likewise describes an outsider falling down to worship and declaring that God is truly among the believers. The captive procession and a prophetic gathering are different settings.

relationship: recognition of Israel's God as Savior
rationale: The confession in Isaiah 45 acknowledges Israel's God as Savior after not knowing Him. Isaiah 43 joins knowing and understanding God with His declaration that no one saves apart from Him. The source does not describe a God hiding Himself.

relationship: internal judgment of opponents through shame
rationale: Isaiah 45 says God's opponents will be ashamed and abashed. Isaiah 41 uses the same paired shame language for those opposing His people; the stated objects of opposition differ.

relationship: Israel's salvation and enduring divine commitment
rationale: Isaiah promises Israel salvation by the Lord without final shame. Romans also speaks of Israel being saved, relating that hope to the Deliverer and God's covenant taking away sins; it develops a distinct argument concerning Gentiles and Israel.

relationship: creation intended for human habitation
rationale: Isaiah says God made the earth to be inhabited rather than empty. Acts identifies the maker of heaven and earth as the One who made humanity to dwell across the earth and appointed the boundaries of dwelling.

relationship: open speech contrasted with secrecy
rationale: The Lord in Isaiah denies speaking secretly or in a dark place. Jesus in John's account likewise says He spoke openly and nothing in secret, directing questioners to His hearers. This compares the explicit public-speech claims without equating their immediate settings.

relationship: carried wooden idols unable to benefit
rationale: Isaiah exposes people carrying a wooden image and praying to gods unable to save. Jeremiah describes wooden manufactured gods that must be carried because they cannot move and have no good in them.

relationship: internal challenge of prediction and unique salvation
rationale: Both passages challenge other claimants to announce what was known from the beginning, then declare the Lord's unique identity and saving power. The combination of announcement, witnesses or assembled hearers, and exclusive salvation grounds the connection.

relationship: universal call to turn to God
rationale: Isaiah calls people at the earth's extremity to turn to God and be saved. Acts rejects manufactured divinity and commands all people everywhere to repent, adding the appointed judgment through the risen Man.

relationship: explicit scriptural citation
rationale: Romans introduces as written the declaration that every knee will bend and every tongue confess to God, matching Isaiah's central wording. Paul uses it to explain each person's accountability at God's judgment seat.

relationship: New Testament reuse of universal homage language
rationale: Philippians repeats the bending of every knee and confession of every tongue in its account of Jesus's exaltation. Isaiah's universal homage to God supplies the corresponding wording; Philippians explicitly names Jesus Christ as Lord and God the Father as glorified.

relationship: internal contrast between divine glory and opponents' shame
rationale: Isaiah 45 sets righteousness and glory coming to Him beside shame for those setting themselves apart. Isaiah 41 likewise announces shame and disappearance for adversaries. The link concerns the opponents' shame, without changing Isaiah 45's pronouns into a personal claim of strength.

relationship: justification joined to glorification by God
rationale: Isaiah joins Israel's offspring being justified from the Lord with being glorified in God. Romans likewise joins God's justifying and glorifying those He calls, within its own account of conformity to His Son.

relationship: named idol's fall and destruction
rationale: Isaiah's actual text names Dagon as shattered. Samuel narrates Dagon falling before the ark and losing head and hands. The shared named idol and its humiliation support the connection without substituting Nebo into Isaiah or identifying the events as one occurrence.

relationship: same-chapter contrast between helpless burdens and saving care
rationale: The burden described across verses 1-2 ends in inability to be saved from war and in captivity. The following address contrasts this with God's own carrying, making and saving of Israel through old age. The reversal of who carries and who can save is explicit in the chapter.

relationship: instruction from childhood
rationale: Isaiah addresses the remnant as instructed from childhood. The psalmist likewise thanks God for teaching him from youth, grounding a lifelong account of God's care.

relationship: divine care into old age
rationale: Isaiah promises God's sustaining and saving presence until advanced age. The psalmist asks God not to forsake him in old age and advanced years. One is an assurance to Israel, the other a prayer for continuing support.

relationship: internal rejection of a manufactured likeness of God
rationale: Both ask to whom the Lord could be likened and immediately contrast Him with human handiwork. Isaiah 40 specifies the craftsman, goldsmith and stabilized wooden image that clarify the kind of comparison being challenged.

relationship: manufactured precious-metal idols
rationale: Isaiah describes measured gold and silver, a hired goldsmith and worship of the handmade result. Jeremiah similarly describes crafted wood adorned with silver and gold and mechanically fastened in place.

relationship: immobility and helplessness of carried idols
rationale: Both expose images that must be lifted and carried because they cannot move themselves. Isaiah adds their inability to hear or save, while Jeremiah denies their ability to do evil or provide good.

relationship: repentance as a return of the heart
rationale: Isaiah calls the wandering to remember, groan, repent and return in heart. Joel likewise summons a whole-hearted return accompanied by mourning and emphasizes the heart rather than merely torn clothing.

relationship: internal declaration that no other god exists
rationale: The call to remember former things leads to God's declaration that none exists beside Him. Isaiah 44 combines the same exclusion of another god with His identity as first and after these things.

relationship: enduring divine counsel
rationale: Isaiah says God's counsel will stand and His plans be accomplished. Proverbs contrasts many human reasonings with the Lord's counsel remaining for ever.

relationship: internal repeated calling and prospering of a journey
rationale: Both passages join God's speaking and bringing the commissioned person with making his journey prosper. Isaiah 46 additionally uses the eastern bird image; that image is not supplied to Isaiah 48.

relationship: same-chapter reversal from far to near righteousness
rationale: The address to people who have lost heart and are far from righteousness is immediately answered by God bringing His righteousness near and not delaying salvation. The repeated righteousness and opposing distance terms make the literary connection explicit, without turning lost heart into a claim of stubbornness.

relationship: internal nearness of salvation
rationale: Isaiah 46 brings righteousness near and says salvation will not delay. Isaiah 56 likewise announces that salvation has drawn near and therefore calls for justice and righteousness; its final clause names the revealing of mercy.

relationship: internal downfall of glorious Babylon
rationale: Isaiah 47 brings pampered daughter Babylon down to the ground and darkness. Isaiah 13 likewise moves glorious Babylon into overthrow and permanent desolation. Both reverse the city's prestige, using different images of the resulting condition.

relationship: grinding as an image of humiliation
rationale: Babylon's fall is pictured through the command to take a millstone and grind flour. Judges narrates captive Samson grinding grain in prison after his capture and blinding. The common labor image marks humiliation, without transferring the blinding or prison details to Babylon.

relationship: city judgment through exposed shame
rationale: Isaiah threatens the uncovering of Babylon's shame in divine justice. Nahum likewise portrays a judged city with its shame and dishonor exposed before nations and kingdoms.

relationship: internal naming of Israel's rescuer
rationale: Both identify the speaking Lord as Israel's Holy One and rescuer or redeemer. Isaiah 43 directly places that identity within action concerning Babylon and the Chaldeans, the city addressed in Isaiah 47.

relationship: internal loss of Babylon's royal standing
rationale: Isaiah 47 says the Chaldean daughter will no longer bear the title of a kingdom's strength. Isaiah 13 describes Babylon's royal glory giving way to uninhabited ruins, a corresponding reversal of its public standing.

relationship: nations exceeding the scope of divine anger
rationale: Isaiah says God handed His people over, but their captor gave no mercy and burdened the elderly. Zechariah likewise distinguishes God's anger from the nations' added assault bringing evils, and announces renewed compassion for Jerusalem.

relationship: failure to consider the end before a city's fall
rationale: Babylon assumes perpetual rule and does not remember the last things. Lamentations similarly says Jerusalem did not remember her last things before being brought exceedingly low. The cities and circumstances differ, while the neglected end is explicit in both.

relationship: confident city's exclusive self-claim
rationale: Both depict a city dwelling confidently and saying in her heart that she alone is and has no counterpart. Zephaniah joins the claim to the city's desolation; Isaiah additionally names Babylon's denial of widowhood and bereavement.

relationship: sudden widowhood and bereavement in judgment
rationale: Isaiah pairs widowhood and childlessness arriving suddenly on Babylon. Jeremiah likewise combines multiplied widows, sudden distress for a mother, and the emptying of a woman who bore seven. Sorcery belongs to Isaiah's setting and is not asserted by Jeremiah here.

relationship: city pride expressed in the repeated I-am claim
rationale: Isaiah repeats Babylon's inward claim that she is and there is no other amid wicked confidence. Zephaniah places the same kind of inward exclusive claim in the mouth of the confident city before its fall.

relationship: unexpected and inescapable destruction
rationale: Isaiah repeatedly warns that destruction will arrive suddenly without Babylon knowing it. Thessalonians likewise places sudden destruction after a declaration of security and says the speakers will not escape. The latter concerns the day of the Lord and does not identify Babylon as its sole subject.

relationship: failure of magical claims to provide help
rationale: Isaiah challenges the long-practiced enchantments and sorcery to help their practitioners. Wisdom similarly exposes magical art and its boasts as helpless, with those promising relief themselves overcome by fear.

relationship: limits of professional divination
rationale: Isaiah challenges heavenly observers to announce what is coming and provide rescue. Daniel denies that disclosure of the royal mystery belongs to wise men and sorcerers and attributes revelation to God. The catastrophe and dream are distinct tests of claimed knowledge.

relationship: judged opponents compared to combustible brush
rationale: Isaiah compares the failed helpers to brushwood burned in fire. Nahum likewise pictures the doomed as a thorn-vine and dry stubble consumed in destruction. Isaiah's taunt about sitting on coals remains its own detail.

relationship: contrast in truthful oath-taking
rationale: Isaiah rebukes those invoking Israel's God without truth or righteousness. Jeremiah gives the positive counterpart: swearing that the Lord lives with truth, judgment and righteousness.

relationship: confidence in a holy place without corresponding conduct
rationale: Isaiah describes people leaning on Israel's God and the holy city's name after exposing false invocation. Jeremiah likewise rebukes confidence in the temple's name while injustice and false oaths continue, requiring changed conduct.

relationship: internal announcement followed by accomplishment
rationale: Both passages place God's prior announcement alongside the arrival or fulfillment of what was announced. Isaiah 48 emphasizes the sudden action; Isaiah 46 relates fulfillment to His enduring counsel.

relationship: stiff-necked resistance
rationale: Isaiah makes the neck an iron sinew as an image of stubbornness. Deuteronomy explicitly calls Israel stiff-necked and recalls continuing wilderness disobedience.

relationship: internal foretelling against rival divine claims
rationale: Isaiah 48 says the prior announcement prevents credit being given to carved or cast images. Isaiah 44 similarly challenges rivals to announce coming things and makes the prior disclosure evidence concerning whether any other god exists.

relationship: internal announcement of new things
rationale: Both announce new things after speaking of earlier things already heard or arrived. Isaiah 48 emphasizes the hearers' failure to understand; Isaiah 42 emphasizes the Lord's advance disclosure.

relationship: same-chapter contrast in claimed prior knowledge
rationale: The earlier verses stress former things announced beforehand, while verse 7 says these things occur now and cannot be claimed as old knowledge. The chapter distinguishes the grounds for knowing God's action and excludes competing claims by idols or hearers.

relationship: faithlessness described from the womb
rationale: Isaiah calls the addressed people lawless from the belly and foretells their rejection of faithfulness. The psalm likewise describes sinners as estranged from the womb and speaking lies from the belly.

relationship: preservation for the divine name's sake
rationale: Isaiah says God will show anger and bring glorious deeds for His name's sake so as not to destroy the people. Ezekiel likewise bases sparing Israel on His profaned name. The comparison does not replace Isaiah's showing anger with delaying anger.

relationship: rescue from a furnace as an image of affliction
rationale: Isaiah names a furnace of poverty from which God rescued the people. Deuteronomy identifies Egypt as the iron furnace from which God brought Israel out. The furnace descriptions differ but both portray rescue from severe subjection.

relationship: internal refusal to give divine glory to another
rationale: Both passages explicitly state that God will not give His glory to another. Isaiah 48 places that refusal beside action for His profaned name; Isaiah 42 additionally names carved images in refusing to give His praiseworthy deeds to them.

relationship: action for the sanctification of a profaned name
rationale: Both explain God's action as undertaken for His own name because His people have profaned it. Ezekiel develops the outcome as the nations knowing the Lord through His sanctification among them.

relationship: internal firstness and enduring divine identity
rationale: Isaiah 48 identifies the caller of Jacob and Israel as first and for ever. Isaiah 44 likewise names Israel's rescuer as first and after these things, with no other god beside Him.

relationship: founding earth and making heaven by God's hands
rationale: Both describe earth as founded by God and heaven as the work of His hands. Isaiah additionally pictures the created things standing together when He calls.

relationship: internal action against Babylon for Israel
rationale: Isaiah 48 connects love for the addressed people with action against Babylon and the Chaldeans. Isaiah 43 likewise promises action in Babylon for Israel's sake and describes the Chaldeans' confinement. Isaiah 48's statement about carrying out your will is preserved.

relationship: internal repeated bringing and prospering
rationale: Both say God brought the commissioned person and made his journey prosper, joining that outcome to His speech. The repeated formulation connects the commissions without importing an additional name into either verse.

relationship: divine sending with the Spirit mentioned
rationale: Isaiah 48 ends with the speaker's sending by the Lord and mention of His Spirit. Isaiah 61 likewise joins the Lord's Spirit upon the speaker with His sending to proclaim good news. The comparison does not decide the grammatical role of the Spirit in Isaiah 48.

relationship: God the Savior teaching the way
rationale: Isaiah identifies the rescuing God as the One showing the road on which His people should walk. The psalm asks God the Savior to make His ways known, teach His paths and guide the petitioner.

relationship: obedience to divine instruction and peace
rationale: Isaiah's conditional lament says listening to His commands would have brought river-like peace. The psalm positively associates loving God's law with great peace; it does not supply Isaiah's river and sea imagery.

relationship: promised descendants compared with sand
rationale: Isaiah describes the offspring that would have multiplied like sand. God's promise to Abraham likewise compares multiplied seed with the sand beside the sea. Isaiah sets the image in an address concerning neglected commands and continuing preservation.

relationship: command to leave Babylon for Zion
rationale: Both summon the people to escape from Babylon. Isaiah explicitly names flight from the Chaldeans and proclamation of Jacob's rescue; Zechariah directs those dwelling in daughter Babylon to escape safely to Zion.

relationship: wilderness water from the rock
rationale: Isaiah promises water brought from a split rock for the people to drink in the wilderness. Exodus narrates the commanded striking of Horeb's rock and the promise that water will come out for the people to drink.

relationship: internal repeated denial of rejoicing to the ungodly
rationale: The declaration that there is no rejoicing for the ungodly recurs at the end of Isaiah 57, following the picture of the unjust tossed by waves and unable to rest. Both supplied texts say rejoicing.

relationship: prophetic calling from the womb
rationale: Isaiah's speaker says the Lord called his name from his mother's belly while addressing nations. Jeremiah likewise receives a calling described as preceding emergence from the womb and appointment as a prophet to nations.

relationship: sharp sword as an image of effective speech
rationale: Isaiah compares the servant's mouth to a sharp sword. Hebrews likewise describes God's active word as sharper than a two-edged sword, developing its penetrating and discerning effect. The comparison concerns speech pictured as a weapon, without equating the speakers.

relationship: internal naming of Israel as God's servant
rationale: Isaiah 49 explicitly names the addressed slave Israel. Isaiah 41 likewise names Israel and Jacob as the servant God chose and called. The cross-reference preserves that named identity rather than silently replacing it.

relationship: labor entrusted to God despite apparent futility
rationale: Isaiah's speaker calls his toil vain but locates his judgment and labor before God. Paul urges steadfast work because labor is not empty in the Lord. The latter supplies an assurance corresponding to the former's appeal, without erasing its lament.

relationship: formation from the womb for divine service
rationale: Isaiah connects formation from the belly with service gathering Jacob and Israel. Jeremiah similarly connects formation and consecration before birth with a prophetic commission, though his stated audience is the nations.

relationship: explicit scriptural reuse in the Gentile mission
rationale: Paul and Barnabas introduce the appointment as a light for Gentiles and salvation to earth's end as the Lord's command for their mission. This repeats Isaiah's light-and-worldwide-salvation formulation; Isaiah additionally names the restoration of Jacob and Israel.

relationship: light and salvation for nations with Israel's glory
rationale: Simeon's declaration joins salvation before all peoples, light for nations and glory for Israel. Isaiah similarly combines the servant's work for Israel with appointment as a light bringing salvation to the earth's extremity.

relationship: homage from kings and rulers
rationale: Isaiah says kings will rise and rulers bow to the chosen figure. The psalm likewise pictures kings presenting gifts and all kings bowing before its royal subject. The connection is the promised homage; the psalm does not supply Isaiah's wording about despising one's own life.

relationship: explicit quotation of the acceptable time
rationale: Paul quotes the acceptable time when God heard and the day of salvation when He helped, matching Isaiah's opening promise. Paul applies it to receiving grace now, while Isaiah continues with covenant and inheritance language.

relationship: internal liberation of prisoners in darkness
rationale: Both describe the commissioned work as releasing those bound and bringing people out of darkness. Isaiah 49 adds their feeding and pasture; Isaiah 42 places release alongside opening blind eyes.

relationship: divine shepherding beside sustaining water
rationale: Isaiah promises that the merciful guide will lead the people through springs without hunger or thirst. The psalm likewise portrays the Lord shepherding, nourishing beside restful water and guiding along paths. It does not repeat the protection from scorching heat.

relationship: internal transformation of difficult terrain into a way
rationale: Isaiah 49 makes mountains roads and paths pasture for the returning people. Isaiah 40 likewise prepares God's way by lowering mountains and making rough country level. Each changes the landscape to permit the promised journey.

relationship: gathering from distant lands and the north
rationale: Isaiah lists arrivals from afar, the north, sea and Persians' land. Jeremiah likewise announces gathering from the north and earth's farthest end. The target supports the distant northern gathering, without replacing Persia with another region.

relationship: internal cosmic rejoicing over Israel's redemption
rationale: Both summon heaven, earth and mountains to rejoice because God has shown mercy to His people. Isaiah 44 explicitly names Jacob's redemption; Isaiah 49 adds comfort for the people's lowly ones.

relationship: lament of being forgotten by God
rationale: Zion says the Lord has forgotten and abandoned her. The psalmist likewise asks how long the Lord will forget him and turn His face away. Both preserve the complaint as the sufferer's speech.

relationship: divine care exceeding parental care
rationale: Isaiah says that even maternal forgetting would not make God forget Zion. The psalm likewise contrasts parental abandonment with the Lord's taking the speaker to Himself. Isaiah poses a maternal possibility; the psalm describes abandonment by both parents.

relationship: internal rebuilding of Zion by unexpected builders
rationale: Isaiah 49 promises rebuilding by those who pulled the city down and departure of its destroyers. Isaiah 60 likewise promises that foreigners will build Zion's walls. Both associate restoration with unexpected human builders, but the passages do not establish that those groups are identical.

relationship: internal summons to see gathered children
rationale: Both command Zion to lift her eyes around and see those gathered to her. Isaiah 60 explicitly names sons and daughters; Isaiah 49 pictures the gathered people as her bridal adornment.

relationship: bridal adornment as an image of restored joy
rationale: Isaiah 49 compares the gathered people worn by Zion to a bride's adornment. Isaiah 61 likewise compares God-given clothing of salvation and joy to bridal ornaments. The adornment's immediate referent differs.

relationship: Jerusalem filled again with inhabitants
rationale: Isaiah says formerly ruined places will be cramped with inhabitants. Zechariah likewise promises fruitful habitation of Jerusalem because of the multitude of people and animals, with God protecting the city.

relationship: internal enlargement for unexpectedly numerous children
rationale: The recovered children in Isaiah 49 complain that their dwelling is too cramped. Isaiah 54 answers the corresponding image of the formerly barren woman's numerous children with commands to widen her tent and spread out.

relationship: internal astonishment at the deserted mother's children
rationale: Isaiah 49 depicts the childless widow wondering who bore and raised the returning children. Isaiah 54 likewise summons the deserted, non-childbearing woman to rejoice because her children are unexpectedly numerous.

relationship: internal return of children carried by others
rationale: Isaiah 49 promises sons brought in bosoms and daughters carried on shoulders. Isaiah 60 repeats the return of sons from afar and daughters lifted upon shoulders, within Zion's gathering.

relationship: royal bowing and dust imagery
rationale: Isaiah pictures rulers bowing to Zion and licking the dust of her feet. The psalm likewise joins kings bowing with enemies licking dust. The groups assigned the dust-licking action differ, while the homage imagery is shared.

relationship: strong man's possessions and the question of plunder
rationale: Isaiah asks whether spoils can be taken from a giant. Jesus similarly asks how someone can seize the strong man's possessions without first binding him. The comparison concerns the obstacle to rescue or plunder; Matthew applies it to His work against demons.

relationship: victory over the strong and taking spoils
rationale: Isaiah connects taking from a strong man with rescue and God's judgment for His people's sons. Luke likewise describes a stronger attacker defeating an armed strong man and distributing his spoils. Luke's setting does not identify the captives named by Isaiah.

relationship: internal recognition of the saving God after reversal
rationale: Both culminate in recognition that the Lord saves or rescues His people. Isaiah 49 reaches that confession through the afflicters' destruction; Isaiah 60 reaches it through the nations' provision and royal wealth. The connection does not transfer self-consuming violence to Isaiah 60.

relationship: divorce imagery for a people's unfaithfulness
rationale: Isaiah asks for the mother's divorce document and explains the sending away through lawless acts. Jeremiah expressly describes Israel receiving a divorce certificate after unfaithfulness. Isaiah's question and its term debtor remain distinct from Jeremiah's narrative.

relationship: internal question about the Lord's saving hand
rationale: Both ask whether God's hand lacks power to save. Isaiah 59 answers by locating separation in the people's offenses; Isaiah 50 likewise surrounds the question with sin, failed response and demonstrations of God's power.

relationship: divine judgment leaving a river's fish dead
rationale: Isaiah describes waters made dry and fish dying for lack of water. Exodus narrates fish dying when the river becomes blood. The common feature is God's judgment on water with dead fish; the mechanism differs and is not harmonized.

relationship: divinely imposed darkness
rationale: Isaiah says God clothes heaven in darkness like sackcloth. Exodus narrates His command for darkness over Egypt. The narrative supplies a concrete counterpart to imposed darkness, without supplying Isaiah's clothing metaphor.

relationship: instruction attributed to the One who sends
rationale: Isaiah's speaker attributes the instructed tongue and listening ear to the Lord. Jesus likewise attributes His teaching to the One who sent Him when hearers question its source. Neither comparison adds a reference to the weary that is absent from Isaiah's supplied wording.

relationship: obedient response to divine instruction
rationale: Isaiah's speaker says the Lord's instruction opens his ears and he does not disobey. Jesus similarly says He always does what pleases the One who sent Him. Both state the speaker's obedience, in different settings.

relationship: spitting and blows upon the face
rationale: Isaiah describes offering cheeks to slaps and not turning the face from spitting. Matthew narrates people spitting into Jesus's face, striking and slapping Him. These particular acts supply the narrative parallel.

relationship: flogging and humiliating treatment of Jesus
rationale: Isaiah joins a back given to scourges with facial humiliation. Matthew narrates Jesus's flogging, mockery, spitting and blows. The correspondence concerns those named acts without claiming Matthew quotes the verse here.

relationship: firmly setting the face toward an ordeal
rationale: Isaiah's speaker sets his face like solid rock in confidence in God's help. Luke describes Jesus firmly setting His face toward Jerusalem as His being taken up approaches. The shared expression depicts determination; Luke does not repeat the rock comparison.

relationship: God's justification against an accuser's charge
rationale: Isaiah pairs the nearness of the One justifying with repeated challenges to anyone bringing a case. Romans likewise asks who can bring a charge or condemn when God justifies, then names Christ's death, resurrection and intercession.

relationship: frailty pictured by a moth-eaten garment
rationale: Isaiah says the opponents will age like a garment and be consumed as by a moth. Job likewise uses the aging or moth-eaten garment image. Isaiah places it within assurance of God's help against harm.

relationship: trust in God while passing through darkness
rationale: Isaiah calls those without light to trust the Lord's name and lean on God. The psalm similarly expresses confidence in God's presence while walking in death's shadow.

relationship: same-chapter contrast between trust and self-kindled light
rationale: Verse 10 calls the person in darkness to trust God; verse 11 addresses people walking by the fire they kindled and ends in sorrow. The neighboring commands contrast the source of reliance and the outcome, without adding an account of a literal fire-setting event.

relationship: same-chapter repeated summons to look at origins
rationale: The command to look at quarried rock and the dug pit is immediately followed by the command to look at Abraham and Sarah, whose one beginning God multiplied. The repeated look frames the ancestral comparison while preserving the active verbs you quarried and you dug.

relationship: Abraham's call and promised multiplication
rationale: Isaiah recalls God calling Abraham when he was one, blessing and multiplying him. Genesis narrates that call with the promise to make Abram a great nation and bless him.

relationship: Sarah's childbearing and descendants from one man
rationale: Isaiah explicitly recalls Sarah's labor and the multiplication of Abraham from one. Hebrews likewise joins Sarah receiving power to conceive with innumerable descendants coming from one aged man.

relationship: restored wasteland compared to a garden
rationale: Isaiah promises to make Zion's deserted places like the Lord's paradise. Ezekiel similarly describes devastated land becoming like a garden of delight and ruined cities standing restored.

relationship: internal outgoing law and judgment for nations
rationale: Isaiah 51 announces law going out from God and judgment as a light for nations. Isaiah 2 likewise describes law going out from Zion and the Lord judging between nations.

relationship: internal hope of nations in divine saving rule
rationale: Isaiah 51 says nations and islands will hope in God's arm as salvation approaches. Isaiah 42 likewise joins judgment established on earth with nations hoping in the servant's name. The objects of the hope are expressed differently.

relationship: aging creation contrasted with divine permanence
rationale: Isaiah compares earth's aging to a garment while declaring everlasting salvation. The psalm likewise says the created heavens and earth grow old like a garment while God remains unchanged. Isaiah's unusual statement about heaven being made firm like smoke is left intact.

relationship: encouragement under human reproach
rationale: Isaiah tells the people with God's law in their heart not to fear human reproach and contempt. Jesus likewise calls His reviled and persecuted followers to rejoice because of their heavenly reward and the prophets' precedent.

relationship: divine instruction held within the heart
rationale: Isaiah identifies the addressed people as having God's law in their heart. The psalmist likewise places God's sayings in his heart so that he may avoid sinning. This connects the inward instruction clause rather than the distinct reproach clause.

relationship: internal recurrence of the moth-eaten garment
rationale: Both use the aging garment and consuming moth for what cannot endure. Isaiah 51 expressly contrasts such decay with God's everlasting righteousness and salvation; Isaiah 50 applies the decay to opponents.

relationship: internal repeated awakening of Jerusalem and Zion
rationale: Both summon Jerusalem or Zion to awake and clothe herself with strength. The addressee in Isaiah 51 is Jerusalem, and the comparison does not introduce a dragon or Rahab absent from its actual wording.

relationship: sea made into a crossing route
rationale: Isaiah recalls the sea depths becoming a road for those rescued. Exodus narrates the sea being dried and split so Israel could enter on dry ground between the waters.

relationship: internal repeated return to Zion with enduring joy
rationale: Both describe those gathered or brought back through the Lord arriving at Zion with everlasting gladness above their heads, while pain and grief depart. The close cluster of wording supports more than a general association with happiness.

relationship: divine reassurance against fear of mortal people
rationale: Isaiah contrasts God's comfort with fear of a mortal human who withers like grass. Jesus likewise discourages fear of those whose power reaches only the body and assures His followers of the Father's care.

relationship: forgetting the God responsible for one's existence
rationale: Isaiah rebukes forgetting the God who made the people and founded creation. Deuteronomy likewise rebukes forsaking the God who begot and nourishes Israel. The creation and parental descriptions differ while the charge of forgetfulness is explicit.

relationship: sea's resounding waves and the Lord's name
rationale: Both identify the Lord by His action causing the sea's waves to resound and give His name as the Lord Sabaoth or Almighty. Jeremiah adds the ordered lights of day and night.

relationship: placing divine words in the commissioned mouth
rationale: Isaiah promises to put God's words in the addressed person's mouth. Jeremiah narrates the Lord touching the prophet's mouth and declaring that He has put His words there.

relationship: judgment pictured as a cup received from God's hand
rationale: Jerusalem has drunk the cup and bowl of anger in Isaiah. Jeremiah receives a cup from the Lord's hand for the nations, whose drinking brings madness before the sword. The shared cup is an image of imposed judgment.

relationship: Jerusalem lacking anyone to comfort her
rationale: Isaiah says none of Jerusalem's children comfort her or take her hand. Lamentations similarly pictures her weeping with no comforter among those who loved her; the identified circle of failed helpers differs.

relationship: crushed Jerusalem asking who can comfort her
rationale: Both describe the daughter's crushing and ask who will comfort her. Lamentations also depicts children failing for want of food, corresponding to Isaiah's named famine and destruction.

relationship: helpless children in the city's public places
rationale: Isaiah depicts exhausted sons lying at the ways out under the Lord's anger. Lamentations likewise depicts children failing in the city squares and pouring out their lives to their mothers. Isaiah's half-boiled-beet simile is not replaced by another animal or image.

relationship: internal drunkenness without wine
rationale: Both explicitly describe a disordered, weakened condition as drunkenness or hangover without wine. Isaiah 51 places that description in the context of the cup of divine anger.

relationship: end of Zion's punishment and transfer of the cup
rationale: Isaiah removes the cup of anger from Jerusalem so she will not drink again. Lamentations similarly ends Zion's lawlessness and deportation while announcing that the Lord's cup will pass to Edom.

relationship: oppressors receiving the cup after Zion
rationale: Isaiah transfers the cup to those who humiliated Jerusalem. Lamentations likewise announces the cup's arrival at Edom while Zion's deportation ends. Isaiah's account of the bowed back as a walkway remains its own description of abuse.

relationship: holiness of Jerusalem and restricted entry
rationale: Isaiah calls Jerusalem the holy city and promises that uncircumcised and unclean people will no longer pass through her. Joel likewise calls Jerusalem holy and says foreigners will no longer pass through; the excluded groups are named differently.

relationship: internal release and reversal of Zion's humiliation
rationale: Isaiah commands captive daughter Zion to rise from dust and remove her neck bond. Isaiah 61 announces release for captives and glory and joy in place of mourning for Zion. The target does not specifically repeat the neck bond.

relationship: ransom distinguished from payment in silver
rationale: Isaiah promises ransom without silver after being sold for nothing. Peter likewise says redemption was not with perishable silver or gold, then names Christ's precious blood. The target supplies its own positive account of redemption's means.

relationship: narrative counterpart to Israel's descent into Egypt
rationale: Isaiah recalls the people's earlier migration to Egypt. Genesis narrates Jacob's household and possessions entering Egypt, naming the children and descendants who went with him.

relationship: narrative counterpart to deportation to Assyria
rationale: Isaiah pairs the earlier stay in Egypt with forcible removal to the Assyrians. Kings records the Assyrian king's capture of Samaria and deportation of Israel, with the places of resettlement.

relationship: explicit citation of God's name blasphemed
rationale: Romans introduces as written the saying that God's name is blasphemed among the nations because of the addressed people. Isaiah contains that same accusation within its lament over the people's captivity.

relationship: recognition of the Lord through His promised rescue
rationale: Isaiah promises that His people will know His name as the One who speaks and is present. Exodus likewise joins the declaration I am the Lord with rescue and the promise that Israel will know Him as their delivering God.

relationship: explicit reuse of the good-news messenger's feet
rationale: Romans introduces a scriptural saying about the beautiful feet of those announcing good things within its argument for sent proclaimers. Isaiah joins the feet of a messenger with peace, good news, salvation and God's reign; the supplied wording is closely related rather than identical throughout.

relationship: close prophetic messenger parallel
rationale: Both bring together mountains, the feet of a good-news bearer and the announcement of peace. Nahum directs Judah to celebrate after the hostile passage has ended; Isaiah announces salvation and God's reign to Zion.

relationship: internal voices of Jerusalem's appointed guards
rationale: Isaiah 52 describes the city's guards raising their voices together at the Lord's mercy. Isaiah 62 likewise appoints guards upon Jerusalem's walls who will not be silent as they remember the Lord, in the context of restoration.

relationship: internal joy of restored deserted places
rationale: Both call attention to Zion or Jerusalem's deserted places receiving divine mercy and renewed joy. Isaiah 51 adds the paradise comparison and thanksgiving; Isaiah 52 specifically names Jerusalem's rescue.

relationship: God's salvation seen at the ends of earth
rationale: Both announce salvation made visible before nations and seen by all earth's ends. The psalm joins that worldwide recognition with remembered mercy to Jacob and Israel.

relationship: scriptural reuse of departure and separation from uncleanness
rationale: Paul repeats the command to come out, be separated and touch nothing unclean in his address to believers as God's temple. Isaiah addresses those carrying the Lord's vessels; that immediate temple-service setting is not erased.

relationship: God leading the departing people
rationale: Isaiah promises that the Lord will go ahead of His people as they depart without turmoil or flight. Exodus narrates God leading the people with the cloud and fire before them. Isaiah's supplied final description names the One gathering them, not a rearguard.

relationship: servant status followed by divine exaltation
rationale: Isaiah announces the servant's exaltation and great glory. Philippians likewise joins Christ's taking a slave's form and humbling Himself with God's highly exalting Him. The comparison does not claim Isaiah states every stage of Paul's account.

relationship: internal repeated description of dishonored appearance
rationale: The servant's form and glory without honor in Isaiah 52 recur in Isaiah 53's absence of form, beauty and honor and the sufferer's being held of no account. The continuation develops the same portrait.

relationship: explicit citation about previously unreached hearers
rationale: Paul quotes the seeing of those not previously told and the understanding of those who have not heard, corresponding to Isaiah's final clause. He applies it to proclaiming Christ where He has not been named; Isaiah also describes the nations' wonder and kings' silence.

relationship: explicit quotation attributed to Isaiah
rationale: John explicitly names Isaiah and quotes both the question about believing the report and the question about the revealed arm of the Lord. He applies the saying to unbelief despite Jesus's signs.

relationship: explicit quotation concerning the received report
rationale: Paul names Isaiah and repeats the question about who believed the report in his discussion of hearing and obedience to the gospel. This corresponds to the first question of the source verse.

relationship: internal repetition of the servant's unhonored appearance
rationale: Isaiah 53 says the figure has no form, glory or beauty; Isaiah 52 already describes the form and glory as without honor among people. The connection concerns that repeated description and leaves the unusual opening We proclaimed before him as a child intact.

relationship: contempt directed at a suffering figure
rationale: Isaiah describes an afflicted figure dishonored and held of no account. The psalm likewise presents a sufferer as an object of human reproach and contempt, mocked by onlookers. Its mockery is not converted into Isaiah's explicit sickness language.

relationship: bearing others' sins and suffering for them
rationale: Isaiah expressly says the figure bears our sins and suffers pain for us. Peter likewise says Christ suffered for the addressed people and bore their sins in His body. The connection follows the actual sin-bearing wording.

relationship: wounding for sins and healing through the wound
rationale: Isaiah links the sufferer's wounds and weakness to the people's sins and says they were healed by his bruise. Peter likewise connects Christ's bearing sins with the declaration that His wound healed the readers.

relationship: reuse of the wandering-sheep comparison
rationale: Isaiah compares everyone straying in their own way to sheep. Peter repeats the comparison for the readers' former wandering and adds their return to the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls.

relationship: explicit reading and interpretation of Isaiah
rationale: Acts identifies the eunuch's reading as Isaiah, quotes the sheep led to slaughter and lamb silent before the shearer, and records Philip beginning with this Scripture to proclaim Jesus. These images match the source's repeated silence.

relationship: narrative counterpart to silence under accusation
rationale: Isaiah depicts the afflicted figure not opening his mouth. Matthew narrates Jesus giving no answer to accusations despite Pilate's questioning, supplying a specific instance of silence under hostile testimony.

relationship: explicit quotation of humiliation and removed judgment
rationale: Acts quotes the removal of judgment in humiliation, the question concerning generation, and life taken from the earth, then records the passage being explained in relation to Jesus. Isaiah additionally explains death through the people's iniquities.

relationship: reuse of the innocent sufferer's lack of deceit
rationale: Peter describes Christ as committing no sin and having no deceit in His mouth, closely matching Isaiah's final clauses. This connection does not turn the source's wicked and rich in exchange wording into an assigned grave with a rich man.

relationship: bearing the sins of many
rationale: Isaiah's verse ends by saying he will bear their sins. Hebrews likewise describes Christ offered once to bear the sins of many. The target supports the sin-bearing clause without replacing Isaiah's statement about justifying the righteous one who serves many well.

relationship: explicit quotation of being counted with the lawless
rationale: Jesus quotes the written saying that He was counted with the lawless and says it must be accomplished in Him. Isaiah explicitly places being numbered among the lawless beside the figure's death and sin-bearing.

relationship: bearing many people's sins in an offering involving death
rationale: Isaiah says the figure's soul was delivered to death and that he bore the sins of many. Hebrews likewise presents Christ as offered once to bear the sins of many, adding His future appearance for salvation.

relationship: explicit citation of the barren woman's many children
rationale: Paul quotes the command to the barren woman to rejoice because the deserted woman's children exceed those of the married woman. He places it in his discussion of the Jerusalem above and children of promise.

relationship: internal enlargement for a growing restored population
rationale: Isaiah 54 commands widening the tent, extending ropes and strengthening pegs after promising numerous children. Isaiah 49 pictures the restored children finding the place too cramped and asking for room to settle.

relationship: multiplied offspring inheriting others' territory
rationale: Isaiah promises offspring inheriting nations and settling deserted cities. Genesis likewise promises Abraham's multiplied seed inheritance of adversaries' cities. The nations and the deserted condition are Isaiah's particular formulations.

relationship: internal reversal of Zion's widowhood and shame
rationale: Isaiah 54 promises that widowhood's reproach will be forgotten and shame need not cause fear. Isaiah 49 likewise moves from Zion's memory of being childless and widowed to returned children, royal service and the assurance that she will not be ashamed.

relationship: worldwide recognition of the Lord's name
rationale: Isaiah identifies Zion's maker and rescuer as the Lord and says He will be called upon throughout the earth. Zechariah similarly places the Lord's kingship and one name over all the earth. Isaiah's source does not call Him husband in this verse.

relationship: internal rejection of abandoned status within marriage imagery
rationale: Isaiah 54 denies that the Lord calls Zion like an abandoned or hated wife. Isaiah 62 likewise says she will no longer be called Abandoned and compares the Lord's joy over her to a bridegroom's joy. Both reject abandonment in this imagery; the source's negative wording is preserved.

relationship: internal movement from judgment to mercy toward Zion
rationale: Isaiah 54 contrasts a short abandonment with great mercy. Isaiah 60 likewise explains the city's restoration by contrasting God's anger in striking with His mercy in loving.

relationship: anger giving way to enduring covenant mercy
rationale: Isaiah contrasts little anger and a turned face with everlasting mercy. Micah likewise says God does not retain anger because He desires mercy, and recalls His sworn mercy to the ancestors.

relationship: explicit appeal to the promise associated with Noah's flood
rationale: Isaiah expressly refers to the water in Noah's time and God's oath as a basis for reassurance. Genesis records the covenant with Noah, his descendants and living creatures that a flood will not again destroy all flesh.

relationship: unremoved and everlasting covenant of peace
rationale: Isaiah says the covenant of peace will never be removed and mercy will not fail. Ezekiel likewise promises a covenant of peace explicitly called everlasting. Isaiah's assurance about mountains and hills is preserved without converting it into their removal.

relationship: explicit prophetic citation of divine teaching
rationale: Jesus introduces as written in the Prophets the saying that all will be taught by God, corresponding to Isaiah's description of the sons. He applies hearing and learning from the Father to coming to Him.

relationship: internal restoration of Zion in righteousness
rationale: Isaiah 54 promises a city built in righteousness and calls for separation from injustice. Isaiah 1 likewise promises restored judges and the name City of Righteousness, joining Zion's salvation with judgment and mercy.

relationship: nations taking refuge with the restored people
rationale: Isaiah promises newcomers approaching through God and taking refuge with the addressed city. Zechariah likewise says many nations will take refuge with the Lord, become His people and dwell within Zion. The native Isaiah wording is positive arrival, not hostile gathering.

relationship: creation's purpose distinguished from destruction
rationale: Isaiah says God is creating the addressed people and did not create them for ruin. Wisdom likewise denies that God made death or delights in destruction and says He created things to exist. Isaiah's contrast with a smith remains distinct from this broader account of creation.

relationship: divine vindication against hostile legal claims
rationale: Isaiah promises defeat of voices raised against the addressed people in judgment and righteousness before God for His servants. Romans similarly asks who can bring a charge or condemn when God justifies. The legal vindication is shared without importing the source's implements into Romans.

relationship: invitation to the thirsty to come and drink
rationale: Isaiah calls the thirsty to water and offers drink without price. Jesus likewise calls anyone thirsty to come to Him and drink; John explains the saying with reference to the Spirit. The source's wine and rich food remain its own features.

relationship: life-giving water offered as a gift
rationale: Isaiah invites those without money to receive water and drink without price. Jesus describes God's gift of living water which He gives and which becomes a spring into eternal life. The connection is the offered sustaining gift, not an identification of ordinary purchased water.

relationship: labor redirected from inadequate food to lasting provision
rationale: Isaiah questions spending money and toil on what fails to satisfy and calls the people to listen and eat good things. Jesus likewise redirects labor from perishing food to the food enduring to eternal life which He gives.

relationship: explicit citation of David's holy and sure blessings
rationale: Acts quotes the holy and sure blessings of David within the proclamation of Jesus's resurrection and the fulfilled ancestral promise. Isaiah names those blessings within God's offer of an everlasting covenant.

relationship: covenant sworn to David with enduring offspring
rationale: Isaiah associates the everlasting covenant with David's sure blessings. The psalm explicitly describes God's covenant and oath to David, promising his offspring and throne through generations.

relationship: royal appointment over nations
rationale: Isaiah speaks of a figure given as ruler and commander of nations following the Davidic blessings. David's song likewise credits God with preserving him as head of nations. The comparison concerns the royal commission without resolving every referent of Isaiah's him.

relationship: response of previously unknown peoples
rationale: Isaiah promises that nations formerly unacquainted with the addressed figure will call and seek refuge. David's song likewise speaks of a people he did not know serving him and foreigners obeying as soon as they hear. The responses are related but not identical.

relationship: seeking, finding and returning to God
rationale: Isaiah commands seeking God and calling when He is found; the following clause joins His drawing near with the call to return. Deuteronomy likewise promises that the people will seek and find the Lord with their whole heart and return to His voice. Isaiah's wording is not changed to while He may be found.

relationship: turning from lawlessness and receiving mercy
rationale: Isaiah calls the lawless to abandon their ways and counsels, return and receive abundant forgiveness. Ezekiel similarly promises life and non-remembrance of transgressions when the lawless turn from their deeds and practice righteousness and mercy.

relationship: divine ways and counsel beyond human understanding
rationale: Isaiah distinguishes God's counsels and ways from those of the hearers. Romans likewise calls His ways untraceable and asks who has known His mind or served as His counselor. It is a conceptual parallel, not an assertion that Romans cites this verse verbatim.

relationship: heaven's height above earth as a measure of divine greatness
rationale: Isaiah uses the distance of heaven from earth to compare God's ways and thoughts with human ones. The psalm uses the same vertical comparison for God's mercy toward those fearing Him. The measured divine qualities differ.

relationship: reuse of seed for the sower and bread for food
rationale: Isaiah describes rain's fruitful result as seed for the sower and bread for food. Paul repeats that paired provision in naming God as supplier and adds multiplication of the readers' seed and fruits of righteousness.

relationship: divine speech accomplished in action
rationale: Isaiah says the word from God's mouth will accomplish His will before returning. Numbers likewise asks whether God would speak and not act or abide by His speech, distinguishing His reliability from human weakness.

relationship: nature personified in joyful response
rationale: Isaiah pictures mountains and hills welcoming with joy and trees clapping branches. The psalm likewise makes rivers clap and mountains exult at God's coming. The images support the connection without changing Isaiah's being taught in joy into being led.

relationship: internal planting of named trees displaying God's work
rationale: Isaiah 55 replaces thorny growth with cypress and myrtle and says the Lord will be for a name and an everlasting sign. Isaiah 41 likewise places cypress and myrtle among trees in formerly waterless land so that people recognize the Lord's action.
